explanations: luna: The section commands the Prophet to tell of the Lord's favor. 2:40 commands Israel to remember “نعمتي التي أنعمت عليكم”; the repeated call makes recollection of received favor a public act of speech and memory. | terra: Israel is commanded to remember the blessing God bestowed, an explicit call to bring divine favor into conscious acknowledgment.

luna: Like 2:40, this ayah commands Israel to remember the favor bestowed on them (“اذكروا نعمتي”). Its repetition reinforces the section's movement from receiving favor to naming it. | terra: The command to remember God’s blessing is repeated with the favor of election, showing that a named blessing carries its giver with it.

luna: The section says the root in “خير” can name asking which of two things is better. After the Israelites ask for other food, 2:61 asks whether they would exchange what is better for what is lower (“أتستبدلون الذي هو أدنى بالذي هو خير”), making that evaluative choice explicit. | terra: A request for different foods is answered by the question whether the people would exchange what is lower for what is better, joining asking with a two-way خَيْر judgment.
terra: The covenant joins good speech to people with material care for parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy, closely matching the section’s union of voice and vulnerability.
terra: The community is warned against asking its Messenger as Moses was culpably asked before, a boundary showing that protecting an asker does not endorse every demand.

luna: This renewed address to Israel again says “اذكروا نعمتي التي أنعمت عليكم.” It is another direct command to recall a divine favor, the act that the section's “فحدث” turns into telling. | terra: A further repetition again binds remembrance of favor to God as its speaker and source.

luna: The section's “السائل” can be someone asking for material help. 2:177 names “السائلين” among those to whom the righteous give wealth, putting care for the asker into the same account of goodness. | terra: Righteous giving expressly includes وَٱلسَّآئِلِينَ, placing petitioners among concrete recipients of wealth.

luna: The section includes someone who comes to ask about God among the meanings of “السائل.” Here worshippers ask the Prophet about God, and the reply says “فإني قريب” and promises response to the caller; the question is met with nearness. | terra: The servants ask the Prophet about God, and God answers without even inserting a command to “say”; this is the clearest questioner received by nearness rather than rebuke.

luna: The section includes the learner who asks within “السائل.” Here people ask the Prophet about the new moons and receive an answer about time-markers for people and pilgrimage, a specific example of a question being answered. | terra: The Prophet is asked about the crescents and receives a direct answer to give, another clear instance of the questioned messenger responding through revelation.

luna: The section says “سأل” can mean asking for something or asking about it. The question “ماذا ينفقون” is answered with whom to support, including orphans and the poor; this joins the questioner's voice to material care. | terra: The question يَسْـَٔلُونَكَ مَاذَا يُنفِقُونَ receives a revealed answer that expressly includes orphans and the needy, joining the section’s questioner and vulnerable petitioner.

luna: This question to the Prophet concerns fighting in the sacred month; the answer distinguishes its gravity from other wrongs. It shows the section's “sā'il” as an inquirer who receives an explanation, not merely a person asking for goods. | terra: The question about fighting in the sacred month is met with a morally differentiated answer rather than dismissal.

luna: People ask about intoxicants and gambling, and the reply weighs their sin against their benefit (“إثمهما أكبر من نفعهما”). This is a particular knowledge-seeker's question within the section's broad sense of “السائل.” | terra: Two questions—about wine and gambling, then what to spend—each receive an answer in the same ayah, displaying repeated question-and-response speech.

luna: The section explicitly treats the question about orphans as a second kind of inquiry. Here “يسألونك عن اليتامى” receives an answer that reforming their affairs is best, showing a questioner met with guidance rather than rebuke. | terra: The question وَيَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلْيَتَـٰمَىٰ is answered with reform and fellowship for orphans, directly meeting both the asking voice and the surah’s protected orphan.
terra: The Prophet is asked about menstruation and is commanded to answer, preserving the questioner even around an intimate subject.

luna: The section's command to tell the Lord's favor meets a direct call to remember “نعمة الله عليكم.” Here the reminder is paired with what God revealed of scripture and wisdom, specifying what the community is to keep in its account. | terra: The community must remember God’s favor and the revealed Book and wisdom by which He instructs them, linking blessing with instructive speech.

terra: God asks Abraham whether he does not believe; Abraham answers بَلَىٰ and explains his request for reassurance, combining an affirmative reply with a petitioner whose further question is received.
terra: Spending is kept sound only when it is not followed by reminders of generosity or injury, setting a speech boundary around aid to the needy.

luna: The section's ban on rebuking a petitioner concerns the words used around need. 2:263 says a kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury (“قول معروف ومغفرة خير”); it makes gentle speech part of giving itself. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are declared better than charity followed by hurt, giving positive speech as the proper answer where material giving may wound.

luna: The section commands speech about the Lord's gift and protects the person who asks from rebuke. 2:264 warns that charity is voided by reminders and injury (“بالمن والأذى”), marking the boundary between grateful telling and speech that wounds a recipient. | terra: Charity can be nullified by reproach and hurt, showing that a giving hand paired with an injuring voice violates the section’s ethic.

luna: The section ties asking for help to the Lord's provision. This neighbor to 2:273 says whatever good people spend is for themselves and will be repaid to them; it completes the context in which the next ayah describes poor people who need support.

luna: The section lets “السائل” mean a needy person who asks at the door. 2:273 describes poor people who “لا يسألون الناس إلحافا” despite their need; it adds the less visible petitioner who does not press people for help. | terra: The restrained poor are described as not asking people insistently, clarifying one kind of petitioner while warning that quiet need can remain unseen.
terra: “Shall I tell you of what is better than that?” combines a comparative خَيْر question with the commanded act of informing.

luna: The section calls this the same reminder given to believers. 3:103 says “واذكروا نعمت الله عليكم” and recalls that God joined their hearts after enmity; recounting the favor includes naming its change in their relationship. | terra: The command to remember God’s blessing then recounts enmity changed into brotherhood and rescue from a fiery brink, modeling favor told as an ordered sequence.
terra: The Prophet’s divinely given gentleness keeps people near, while harshness would scatter them; this explains the human consequence of a rebuking voice.
terra: Those managing another’s property must provide food and clothing and say قَوْلًا مَّعْرُوفًا, pairing care with fitting words.
terra: When relatives, orphans, and the needy attend a distribution, they are to receive provision and قَوْلًا مَّعْرُوفًا, pairing material care with honorable speech.
terra: Instead of coveting unequal allotments, people are commanded to ask God for His bounty, redirecting petition toward the giver.
terra: Worldly enjoyment is called little and the Hereafter خَيْر for the God-fearing, a close formulation of 93:4’s comparison.
terra: The rhetorical question وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ حَدِيثًا grounds trustworthy speech in God, complementing the section’s concern with rightly sourced telling.
terra: The repeated question وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ قِيلًا supplies a nonlexical parallel: divine promise is the truest speech.

luna: The section says “سأل” includes asking about something. This ayah explicitly says people ask the Prophet for a ruling about women and orphans; the reply attends to their rights, a concrete inquiry met with guidance. | terra: People seek the Prophet’s ruling concerning women, and God answers with a ruling that expressly protects orphan girls, linking inquiry with vulnerable dependents.
terra: The People of the Book demand a book from heaven and are recalled as having asked Moses for something still greater, exemplifying coercive questioning rather than teachable inquiry.

luna: The opening “يستفتونك” presents people asking the Prophet for a ruling about inheritance, and he answers them. It is another specific instance of the knowledge-seeker included by the section's broad sense of “السائل.” | terra: People seek a ruling and God commands the Prophet to give the ruling on inheritance, a nonlexical parallel to the question-and-answer office.

luna: The question “ماذا أحل لهم” asks the Prophet what is lawful, and he answers with good things and trained hunting animals. It gives a concrete case of the learner's question being answered. | terra: The question about what is lawful is answered with a revealed ruling, another direct يَسْـَٔلُونَكَ / قُلْ exchange.

luna: This ayah commands believers to remember “نعمت الله عليكم” together with their covenant. It is another explicit communal recollection of God's favor, matching the section's move from private gift to voiced recognition. | terra: The command to remember divine favor is joined to the covenantal words “we hear and obey,” so remembered grace and a spoken response meet.

luna: Believers are told to remember God's favor when a people meant to reach out against them and God restrained their hands. This gives the section's command a concrete account of protection to tell. | terra: Believers are told to remember God’s favor when He restrained hostile hands, a concise example of naming a specific rescue as His gift.
terra: Moses tells his people to remember God’s favor and then lists prophethood, kingship, and unprecedented gifts, modeling enumerated blessing in direct address.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite truthfully the report of Adam’s two sons, a direct counterpart to the command to tell.
terra: Believers are told not to ask questions whose disclosed answers would distress them, marking a substantive limit on questioning without licensing harsh treatment of people.
terra: Earlier people asked such questions and then rejected their answers, supplying the failure that explains the warning in 5:101.

luna: The section quotes God's command to Jesus to remember His favor on him and his mother (“اذكر نعمتي عليك وعلى والدتك”). It is a direct parallel to publicly acknowledging a received divine blessing. | terra: God commands Jesus to remember His favor to him and his mother and then enumerates its forms, an explicit divine model for recounting the Lord’s blessing.
terra: When the condemned are asked whether the encounter is true, they answer بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا, an affirmative response that explicitly names their Lord.
terra: The home of the Hereafter is said to be better for the mindful than worldly play and diversion.

luna: Like 18:28, this ayah forbids driving away people who call on their Lord (“ولا تطرد الذين يدعون ربهم”). It gives a second direct counterpart to the section's command not to rebuke the person who comes seeking. | terra: The Prophet is forbidden to drive away humble people who call on their Lord, directly protecting low-status seekers from exclusion.
terra: The Prophet must leave mockers of revelation until they enter a different حَدِيث, showing that conversation has moral boundaries and can be replaced by another.

luna: The section says the three gifts include guidance and commands that the Lord's favor be told. The people of Paradise say “الحمد لله الذي هدانا لهذا” and acknowledge they would not have been guided without God; this voices guidance as a gift from its giver. | terra: The people of Paradise praise God for guiding them and say they could not have been guided without Him, a faithful spoken attribution of saving favor.

luna: The section notes that the root of “بنعمة” also yields “نعم,” an affirmative answer. In 7:44 the people of the Fire answer “نعم” when asked whether they found God's promise true, giving that response word its explicit Quranic scene. | terra: One side asks whether God’s promise proved true and the other answers نَعَمْ; the word functions at once as answer, confirmation, and recognition of a fulfilled promise.
terra: A people are commanded to remember the favors that made them successors and increased them in stature, turning history and embodiment into named divine gifts.
terra: Another people are commanded to remember becoming successors and being settled in the land, again attaching received conditions to their giver.
terra: Pharaoh’s magicians ask whether they will be rewarded if victorious, supplying the question to which 7:114 gives the section’s affirmative-answer word.
terra: Pharaoh replies نَعَمْ and adds a promise of nearness, exactly illustrating “yes” as answer, confirmation, and promise after 7:113.
terra: The question “Am I not your Lord?” receives the affirmative بَلَىٰ and testimony, a Quranic affirmative form answering a negative question.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite a person’s report so that hearers may reflect, explicitly assigning a purpose to narration.

luna: People ask the Prophet about the Hour, but he answers that its knowledge rests with his Lord. This shows a questioner met with an answer that sets a boundary on what can be told. | terra: The Prophet is asked about the Hour and commanded to state that its knowledge belongs to his Lord, an answer that also marks the limit of what he can tell.

luna: The question “يسألونك عن الأنفال” asks about the division of spoils, and the answer calls for God-consciousness and reconciliation. This combines a request about material goods with an answer that redirects the question toward conduct. | terra: A question about spoils receives a command to answer by assigning them to God and the Messenger and redirecting the community toward reconciliation.
terra: The believers are told to remember being few and vulnerable before God sheltered, strengthened, and provided them, a striking parallel to the three successive favors in surah 93.
terra: The ayah asks whether people prefer worldly life to the Hereafter and declares worldly enjoyment slight by comparison.

luna: The questioners ask whether the warning is true, and the Prophet is told to answer “إي وربي إنه لحق.” This joins the section's inquirer with an affirmative spoken reply, though the ayah uses “إي” rather than the source's lexical “نعم.” | terra: A question asks whether the promised event is true and the Prophet is commanded to answer إِى وَرَبِّى, an affirmative reply explicitly grounded in his Lord.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite Noah’s report, another repeated formulation of divinely ordered telling.
terra: Noah says he asks no wealth, assigns his reward to God, and refuses to drive believers away, joining non-demanding prophetic speech with protection of socially dismissed hearers.
terra: Noah is told not to ask God for what he lacks knowledge of, a boundary on the petitioner’s claim grounded in truth rather than social status.
terra: God tells the Prophet that messenger accounts are narrated to steady his heart and bring truth, admonition, and reminder, explaining what sequential telling produces.
terra: God says He narrates أَحْسَنَ ٱلْقَصَصِ through revelation, a direct model of beautiful, unfolding narration.

luna: The section defines “حديث” as speech from which one thing follows another. 12:6 promises Joseph the interpretation of “الأحاديث”; the plural ties the root to accounts and unfolding meanings, though here it concerns dreams. | terra: Jacob says God will teach Joseph the interpretation of ٱلْأَحَادِيثِ and complete His blessing upon him and his family, bringing the roots of narration and favor together in one promise.
terra: Joseph and his brothers are said to contain signs for ٱلسَّآئِلِينَ, treating questioners as people to whom a narrated story yields knowledge.

luna: Joseph is promised “تأويل الأحاديث” in this account of his life. The root's sense of unfolding report or interpretation meets the section's account of speech that brings one thing after another. | terra: Joseph’s establishment in the land is linked to being taught the interpretation of ٱلْأَحَادِيثِ, extending the root from spoken reports to meaningful dreams or events.
terra: Joseph asks whether scattered lords are خَيْر or the one overpowering God, a direct question seeking the better of two alternatives.

luna: The section gives Joseph's words as an example of attributing kindness to God: “وقد أحسن بي” when God brought him out of prison. His reunion account names the good he received, illustrating what it means to tell of a Lord's favor. | terra: Joseph himself says his Lord treated him well by bringing him from prison and reuniting his family, narrating grace while assigning it to its true giver.

luna: Joseph asks God to teach him the interpretation of “الأحاديث” after the story's events have unfolded. This links the root's narrative sense to a speaker making sense of what has happened. | terra: After the reunion in 12:100, Joseph addresses his Lord and names the rule and interpretive knowledge given to him, continuing faithful first-person narration of gifts.
terra: The home of the Hereafter is said to be better for those who are mindful, repeating the later-life comparison.

luna: Moses tells his people to remember God's favor when He saved them from Pharaoh's people. Like the section's sequence of shelter, guidance, and provision, this is a narrated deliverance offered as a divine favor. | terra: Moses tells his people to remember God’s blessing in rescue from Pharaoh’s people, an explicit prophetic retelling of favor.
terra: God’s proclamation promises increase for gratitude and warns of punishment for ingratitude, stating what follows from the response to favor.
terra: Those who exchange God’s blessing for unbelief transform received favor into ruin, a reversal of grateful narration.

luna: The section presents three blessings in sequence before commanding their telling. 14:34 says God's favors cannot be enumerated (“لا تحصوها”); it widens that short sequence into an uncountable abundance to acknowledge. | terra: God gives people from all they ask and immediately says His blessing cannot be counted, bringing request, provision, and the enumeration of favor into one ayah.
terra: Abraham praises God for granting Ishmael and Isaac in old age, a concise first-person telling of answered gift.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to inform people about Abraham’s guests, after which their encounter unfolds in successive speech.

luna: Like 14:34, this ayah says God's favors cannot be counted (“لا تحصوها”). It gives the section's command to tell of favor an open-ended subject rather than a closed list. | terra: The assertion that people cannot count God’s blessings sets a limit around the section’s exemplary enumeration: telling can name gifts without exhausting them.
terra: Those who answer well say their Lord sent good, and the home of the Hereafter is declared better, joining answer and خَيْر.

luna: The section allows “السائل” to be a learner asking a question. 16:43 directs those who do not know to ask people of remembrance (“فاسألوا أهل الذكر”), giving that sense of the protected questioner a concrete place in seeking knowledge. | terra: Those who do not know are commanded فَسْـَٔلُوٓا۟ أَهْلَ ٱلذِّكْرِ, legitimizing the learner who approaches a knowledgeable person with a question.

luna: The section commands the Prophet to tell of “نعمة ربك.” 16:53 says that whatever favor people have is from God (“وما بكم من نعمة فمن الله”), giving the attribution that the command asks the speaker to preserve. | terra: Whatever blessing people possess is said to be from God, stating the attribution that the phrase “your Lord’s blessing” preserves.

luna: The section contrasts proper telling of the Lord's favor with a false claim of ownership. 16:83 says people recognize God's favor and then deny it (“يعرفون نعمت الله ثم ينكرونها”), a direct reversal of voicing it. | terra: People recognize God’s blessing and then deny it, the opposite of telling the favor while faithfully naming its source.
luna: The section connects blessing with a voiced response; 16:114 commands people to eat from God's provision and “اشكروا نعمت الله.” It makes gratitude the fitting answer to a received favor.
terra: The command to call with wisdom, good exhortation, and the best manner of argument gives concrete qualities to the constructive voice that replaces rebuke.

luna: The section's verb “تَنْهَرْ” means to rebuke. In 17:23 children are told not to rebuke their parents (“ولا تنهرهما”) and instead to speak nobly; this supplies a concrete boundary for the same harsh verbal act. | terra: The identical prohibition فَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا protects aged parents from a harsh voice, clarifying what the section’s تَنْهَرْ forbids toward an asker.

luna: When someone must turn away from people seeking the Lord's mercy, 17:28 still commands “فقل لهم قولا ميسورا”—a gentle, accessible word. This gives the section's asker a specific model of response when the request cannot be granted. | terra: When one must turn away from needy recipients, the command is still to speak قَوْلًا مَّيْسُورًا, directly protecting the petitioner from a hard refusal.
terra: God’s servants are commanded to say what is best because Satan creates discord between people, supplying a positive rule for the voice that replaces harsh speech.
terra: When favored, the human turns aside; when touched by evil, he despairs, the opposite of receiving favor and then speaking grateful acknowledgment.

luna: People ask about the spirit; the answer says it is from the Lord's command and that human knowledge is limited. This is a specific question answered with a boundary, like 7:187's question about the Hour. | terra: The question about the spirit is answered with a bounded statement of divine command and limited human knowledge.

luna: The section commands “فلا تنهر” toward the asker. 18:28 likewise says not to drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening (“ولا تطرد الذين يدعون ربهم”), directly extending protection to devoted seekers. | terra: The Prophet must remain patiently with those who call on their Lord and must not look past them toward worldly adornment, closely paralleling the status reversal in the seeker scene.
terra: The garden owner boasts that he is greater in wealth and followers, supplying the self-magnifying speech corrected by 18:39.
terra: He enters his garden wronging himself and claims it will never perish, treating the gift as self-secured rather than entrusted.
terra: He speculates that even if returned to his Lord he will find something خَيْر, misusing “better” to extend entitlement into the Hereafter.

luna: The section contrasts telling that a gift belongs to the Lord with the claim “هذا لي” in 41:50. In 18:39 the companion tells the garden owner to say “ما شاء الله لا قوة إلا بالله,” a specific correction to self-reliance when entering a place of wealth. | terra: His companion supplies the missing speech, مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِ, teaching how the garden should have been verbally attributed.
terra: Moses courteously asks to follow Khidr so he can be taught, a fully staged learner’s request that leads to the speech rule in 18:70.
terra: Khidr answers Moses’s request with a candid warning about patience rather than contempt, beginning the negotiated teacher-seeker relation.
terra: Khidr tells Moses not to ask until he himself says حَتَّىٰ أُحْدِثَ لَكَ مِنْهُ ذِكْرًا; asking and the root of telling meet in one pedagogical rule.
terra: Moses himself accepts that another question will end his companionship with Khidr, a negotiated pedagogical boundary after repeated breaches.

luna: The section's root note says “سأل” covers asking to know as well as asking to receive. Here people ask the Prophet about Dhul-Qarnayn, and he is to answer by reciting a remembrance of him (“سأتلوا عليكم منه ذكرا”), joining the questioner with the narrator. | terra: People ask the Prophet about Dhu al-Qarnayn and he answers, سَأَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْكُم مِّنْهُ ذِكْرًا, turning a question into an unfolding account.
terra: Disbelievers ask which of the two groups is خَيْر in station and assembly, illustrating a two-way “better” question distorted by worldly status.

luna: The section says telling is a form of Quranic address and quotes “وهل أتاك حديث موسى.” The ayah opens Moses' story by asking the Prophet whether its account has reached him, making narrated report itself a mode of address. | terra: The question وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ makes an interrogative voice the opening through which a narrative is told.
terra: Moses begins the extended request answered in 20:36 by asking his Lord to expand his breast; this is the first concrete content of his سُؤْل.
terra: He asks that his task be made easy, a second element of the petition granted as a whole in 20:36.

luna: The section treats speaking as an act that may unfold from one utterance to another. In Moses' prayer he asks God to loosen the knot in his tongue (“واحلل عقدة من لساني”), naming an impediment to the speech he is about to deliver. | terra: He asks for the knot in his tongue to be loosened, making the long petition itself partly a request for an effective voice.

luna: Moses' neighboring prayer asks that the people understand his speech (“يفقهوا قولي”). It connects the section's command to tell with the speaker's aim that his words be received clearly. | terra: The requested loosening is so people may understand his speech, stating the intended result of the voice requested in 20:27.
terra: Moses next asks for a minister from his family, another distinct item in the request answered at 20:36.
terra: He identifies Aaron as the brother requested for that role, specifying the person included in his petition.
terra: Moses asks that Aaron strengthen his back, adding the requested function to the long prayer.
terra: He asks that Aaron share his task, completing the practical request that precedes 20:36.
terra: Moses gives abundant glorification as one purpose of the requested help, moving the petition toward the speech it is meant to enable.
terra: He adds abundant remembrance of God, another speech-purpose embraced by the grant in 20:36.
terra: The prayer closes by acknowledging God’s constant sight of them, immediately before the compact answer in 20:36.

luna: The section's “سائل” can be one who asks for something. After Moses' long supplication, God answers “قد أوتيت سؤلك يا موسى”; this is a direct instance of a request received and granted. | terra: God answers Moses’s extended petition with the compact assurance قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ, a request met by granting rather than harshness.

luna: After the answer to Moses' request in 20:36, God says “ولقد مننا عليك مرة أخرى” and begins recalling an earlier favor. This neighbor completes the section's connection between a granted request and an account of prior blessing. | terra: Immediately after granting the request in 20:36, God begins to recount an earlier favor, so answered asking gives way to the telling of grace exactly as in the section.
terra: The favor-story announced in 20:37 begins with revelation to Moses’s mother, the first event in the sequential telling.
terra: God recounts the chest, river, enemy household, bestowed love, and watchful care, making several protective favors emerge one after another.
terra: The recounting continues through his sister, restoration to his mother, rescue from killing, trial, years in Midian, and measured arrival, an extended model of narrating grace sequentially.

luna: The section forbids a harsh verbal response to the asker. Moses and Aaron are told to speak gently to Pharaoh (“فقولا له قولا لينا”); though the addressee differs, the ayah makes gentleness a commanded way of speaking. | terra: Moses and Aaron must speak gently even to Pharaoh so he might remember or fear, an emphatic boundary against harsh address.
terra: The magicians declare God better and more lasting than Pharaoh, voicing the preferable of two allegiances under threat.
terra: God says He recounts reports of what preceded and has given the Prophet a reminder, another direct divine description of narrative address.

luna: People ask the Prophet about the mountains, and the answer describes them being scattered away. It is another concrete instance of the questioner's voice receiving an answer in the Quran. | terra: The Prophet is asked about the mountains and told exactly how to answer, turning inquiry into revealed description.
terra: The Arabic Quran varies warnings so that it may يُحْدِثُ لَهُمْ ذِكْرًا, letting speech bring forth a new act of remembrance.
terra: Every newly arriving reminder is heard while people play, showing speech that produces no attentive “thing after thing” because its hearers trivialize it.

luna: Like 16:43, this ayah tells those who do not know to ask people of remembrance (“فاسألوا أهل الذكر”). It directly supports the section's learner who comes with a question, rather than a material petition. | terra: The same command to ask the people of remembrance if one does not know directly dignifies inquiry as the proper response to ignorance.
terra: God is not questioned about what He does while people will be questioned, marking the ultimate asymmetry within the root’s otherwise reciprocal possibilities.
terra: Sacrificial meat is to feed both the contented person and the one who asks, a material answer to distinct forms of need.
terra: Noah is instructed to praise God after being delivered from wrongdoers, turning rescue into an explicit spoken acknowledgment.
terra: Messengers and peoples follow one another in succession and the destroyed peoples become أَحَادِيثَ, joining “one thing after another” with the stories left by events.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to repel evil with what is best, a concise rule for replacing an injurious voice with a better response.
terra: At the trumpet blast people لَا يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, a direct negation of reciprocal questioning when ordinary relationships collapse.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to ask whether that punishment is خَيْر or the promised eternal Garden, an explicit two-alternative question about the better outcome.
terra: The addressee is told to ask one who is informed about the Merciful, another explicit validation of inquiry directed to knowledge.
terra: When the ignorant address the servants of the Merciful, they answer with peace, modeling a restrained reply even under provocation.
terra: Each renewed reminder from the Merciful is met by turning away, the reception opposite both listening to a questioner and responding to a divine account.
terra: Pharaoh recounts raising Moses and his years in the household as leverage in an accusation; 26:22 identifies this weaponized account as a claimed “favor.”
terra: Pharaoh cites his upbringing of Moses as a “favor” used to reproach and control him; Moses exposes how telling a benefit can itself become injurious speech.
terra: The magicians ask Pharaoh about a reward, setting up the affirmative promise in 26:42 and repeating the section’s question-and-answer structure.
terra: The reply نَعَمْ confirms the requested reward and promises favored proximity, realizing all the answer-functions developed for the word.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to recite Abraham’s report, repeating the stance of a divinely instructed narrator.
terra: Abraham begins an ordered first-person account: the Lord who created him is the one who guides him.
terra: Abraham next names God as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, continuing the narrated benefits.
terra: He next attributes healing during illness to God, adding another concrete favor to the sequence.
terra: He then names death and restored life as God’s acts, extending the account beyond present provision.
terra: The sequence culminates in Abraham’s hope that his Lord will forgive his fault on Judgment Day.
terra: Noah states that he will not drive believers away, a direct nonlexical counterpart to receiving the vulnerable person without rebuke.
terra: David and Solomon turn knowledge into spoken praise of God who favored them, a faithful verbal attribution of an intellectual gift.

luna: The section connects telling a Lord's favor with voiced acknowledgment. Solomon asks God to enable him to be grateful for “نعمتك التي أنعمت علي”; this is a direct spoken response to a received favor. | terra: Solomon asks to be enabled to thank God for the blessing bestowed on him and his parents, making favor the content of prayerful speech.
terra: Solomon says what God has given him is better than the envoys’ gift, combining correct divine attribution with a خَيْر comparison.

luna: The section contrasts naming the Lord as giver with the claim “هذا لي” in 41:50. When Solomon receives the throne, he says “هذا من فضل ربي”; the explicit attribution makes this a positive counterpart to claiming a favor as one's own. | terra: Solomon answers the arrival of the throne with هَـٰذَا مِن فَضْلِ رَبِّى and names it a test of gratitude, a precise model of attributing favor to its Lord.
terra: The commanded question ءَآللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ is the most compact Quranic instance of asking which of two is better.

luna: The section's examples include God answering a questioner and Moses receiving what he asked. 27:62 asks who answers the distressed person when he calls and removes hardship; it makes divine response to the needy caller explicit.

luna: The section presents Moses turning a received blessing into speech: “رب بما أنعمت علي” precedes his pledge not to aid wrongdoers. The ayah shows a blessing being acknowledged aloud and shaping what the speaker will do. | terra: Moses turns أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَىَّ into a spoken pledge never to support criminals, showing remembered favor generating a new word and commitment.

luna: The section recalls Moses' request and God's answer in 20:36. Here Moses, in need, says “إني لما أنزلت إلي من خير فقير”; the prayer for whatever good God sends makes the speaker both a petitioner and a recipient of provision.
terra: When believers hear harmful speech, they turn away and answer with a peaceable boundary rather than reciprocal abuse.
terra: Worldly goods are contrasted with what is with God, which is better and more lasting.
terra: On the Day of Judgment answers become obscure and people do not ask one another, reversing the section’s living exchange of question and response.

luna: The section's dictionary note connects “خير” with seeking the better of two things. 28:68 uses the related choice form “يختار” and “الخيرة,” while saying creation and choice belong to God; it makes choice the boundary of human asking. | terra: The Lord creates and chooses, while people do not possess the choice, grounding the خ ي ر family’s selection-sense in divine agency.

luna: The section commands the recipient to tell of the Lord's favor. Qarun's people tell him to use what God granted for the Hereafter and “أحسن كما أحسن الله إليك”; this gives an explicit response to received favor that contrasts with claiming it as one's own in 28:78.

luna: The section calls “هذا لي” a false account of favor. Qarun answers his people's reminder that God granted him wealth by claiming it came from his own knowledge (“على علم عندي”); neighboring 28:77 supplies the reminder he rejects. | terra: Qarun claims his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, the same self-crediting distortion that the section opposes.
terra: Dispute with the People of the Book must use the best manner except toward persistent wrongdoers, specifying both gentle speech and its boundary.
terra: If the deniers are asked who created the heavens and earth and subjected sun and moon, they answer “God,” a question eliciting true attribution despite inconsistent conduct.
terra: If asked who sends rain and revives the earth, they answer “God,” making a question draw out acknowledgment of the giver of provision.
terra: People enjoy a secure sanctuary yet believe falsehood and deny God’s blessing, suppressing the gift’s true attribution.
terra: Idle or misleading لَهْوَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ is purchased to divert people from God’s way, a specific reversal of speech that gives rise to guidance.
terra: The command to lower one’s voice and the comparison with the harsh donkey-call add vocal manner to the section’s concern with what a voice does to its hearer.
terra: If asked who created the heavens and earth, they answer “God,” and the Prophet is told to praise God, converting their answer into the fitting response.

luna: The address “اذكروا نعمة الله عليكم” recalls the day the enemy forces came and God sent wind and unseen forces. This is a concrete communal story of protection that gives content to speaking of the Lord's favor. | terra: Believers are commanded to remember God’s favor when armies came and unseen forces repelled them, naming deliverance as divine gift.
terra: Guests are forbidden to linger for حَدِيث after a meal, showing the root’s ordinary social-conversation sense and the boundaries proper to it.

luna: People ask about the Hour, and the answer says its knowledge is with God and that it may be near. The question receives both a limit and a warning, specifying the section's question-and-answer relation. | terra: People ask the Prophet about the Hour and he is told to answer that its knowledge is only with God.
terra: After disbelievers deny that the Hour will come, the Prophet is commanded to answer بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّى, an affirmation grounded in his Lord and followed by a promise.

luna: The section commands telling of the Lord's favor; 35:3 tells people to remember God's favor and asks who else provides from heaven and earth. The ayah joins naming the blessing with naming its giver. | terra: Humanity is commanded to remember God’s blessing and asked whether any creator besides Him provides from heaven and earth, grounding narration in the true giver.

luna: The section's command is to voice recognition of the Lord's favor. The people of Paradise say “الحمد لله الذي أذهب عنا الحزن,” directly voicing thanks for a deliverance they have received. | terra: The people of Paradise praise God who removed sorrow from them, narrating their changed condition while naming its giver.
luna: This neighbor completes the praise in 35:34 by naming God's grace as the reason they were settled in the lasting home (“من فضله”). It adds the specific favor behind their spoken thanks.
terra: When told to spend from God’s provision, disbelievers answer with a contemptuous refusal to feed the needy, staging the harsh voice opposite the section’s command.
terra: This ayah poses the resurrection question to which 37:18 gives the commanded نَعَمْ, contributing the primary interrogative.
terra: The added question about forefathers extends the challenge that the affirmative answer in 37:18 resolves.

luna: The section's lexical note links “نعمة” with the response “نعم.” In 37:18 “نعم” answers whether resurrection will occur, making the yes-sayer a distinct voice in a scene of questioning. | terra: The command قُلْ نَعَمْ supplies the terse affirmative answer to the resurrection questions in 37:16 and 37:17.

luna: The section notes that asking can be mutual (“تساءلوا”). 37:27 says the guilty turn to one another, asking and blaming each other; this is a contrary use of mutual questioning, unlike a petitioner who should not be rebuked. | terra: The condemned turn to one another يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, preserving the reciprocal-question sense in a scene whose ensuing dialogue exposes mutual blame.

luna: The section notes that asking may be reciprocal (“تساءلوا”). 37:50 shows the people of Paradise turning toward one another to ask; 37:51 begins one speaker's account, bringing the section's mutual questioning and telling together. | terra: The people of Paradise turn to one another يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, after which one speaker’s story emerges detail by detail.

luna: This neighbor continues the mutual conversation in 37:50: one of them begins, “إني كان لي قرين.” Its own contribution is a speaker starting an account in response to their turning toward one another. | terra: A speaker arising from the mutual questioning in 37:50 begins, “I had a companion,” giving the first item in the ensuing sequential account.
terra: The remembered companion’s skeptical question is quoted inside the Paradise conversation, making one dialogue generate another narrated dialogue.
terra: A second quoted question completes the companion’s challenge about resurrection, extending the story that grew from 37:50.
terra: The speaker asks his present companions whether they will look, moving the reciprocal exchange to its next action.
terra: He looks and sees the former companion in the Fire, supplying the discovered consequence about which his story continues.
terra: He addresses the companion and says he nearly brought about his ruin, interpreting the danger just shown in 37:55.
terra: The account culminates, “Were it not for my Lord’s blessing,” explicitly assigning deliverance to the Lord within a conversation generated by mutual questioning.
terra: The ayah asks whether the Garden’s hospitality is خَيْر or the tree of Zaqqum, another explicit binary “better” question.
terra: David judges that one partner wronged another by asking for his ewe to add to many, a concrete case in which a request itself becomes exploitative.
terra: Iblis says “I am better than him,” turning خَيْر comparison into arrogant self-valuation rather than a sincere search for the better.
terra: A distressed person calls on his Lord, but after receiving a blessing forgets the earlier prayer and assigns rivals to God.
terra: Those who listen to speech and follow its best are praised, connecting the section’s good speaker with discernment among spoken alternatives.
terra: God calls the revelation أَحْسَنَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ, a Quranic realization of the source section’s dictionary phrase for fine or beautiful speech.
terra: If asked who created the heavens and earth, the deniers answer “God,” after which the Prophet exposes the powerlessness of their other objects of appeal.
terra: After God confers a favor, the person claims it was given because of his own knowledge; this directly exposes the distorted telling corrected by 93:11.
terra: The inheritors of Paradise praise God for fulfilling His promise and granting them the land, combining fulfilled promise, gift, and verbal acknowledgment.

luna: The section includes a prayer answered with “قد أوتيت سؤلك” and God's promise of nearness to the caller. 40:60 gives the direct call-and-response formulation, “ادعوني أستجب لكم,” as another statement that a seeker may address God and receive an answer. | terra: God commands people to call upon Him and promises to answer, presenting the petitioner as invited and the response as assured.

terra: The earth’s provisions are measured سَوَآءً لِّلسَّآئِلِينَ; if “askers” carries its ordinary petitioner sense here, it depicts provision prepared for all who seek it, though it may instead mean those needing or inquiring about it.

luna: The section notes the dictionary description of a person whose speech is good (“حسن الحديث”). 41:33 praises the one whose speech is best, calling to God and acting righteously; it gives a concrete Quranic counterpart for speech valued by its content. | terra: The ayah asks who is better in speech than one who calls to God, does right, and openly identifies as submitted, defining excellent speech by source and effect.
terra: Evil is to be repelled with what is better, so the manner of response can transform hostility into intimacy.
terra: The question contrasts one cast into the Fire with one who arrives secure and asks which is خَيْر, using comparison to force moral discernment.

luna: The section calls this a crooked account of favor: after relief, the speaker says “هذا لي,” claiming the gift as his own. It reverses the command to name it as “نعمة ربك” and shows what grateful telling corrects. | terra: After mercy following hardship, the person says هَـٰذَا لِى, assigning the gift to himself instead of naming it as his Lord’s favor.

luna: The section uses 41:50 as a crooked account of favor, where the speaker says “هذا لي.” Its neighbor 41:51 adds the response after a gift—turning away—and after harm—making extended supplication—completing the contrast with telling of the Lord's favor. | terra: After the false claim in 41:50, favor makes the person turn away while harm produces prolonged supplication, exposing the distorted relation between gift and voice.
terra: Worldly provision is temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for believers.
terra: A tasted mercy produces self-satisfaction, while adversity exposes human ingratitude, another specific reversal of the response appropriate to favor.
terra: If asked who created the heavens and earth, the deniers answer that the Mighty, Knowing One created them.

luna: The section asks the speaker to tell of the Lord's favor. When travelers mount what carries them, they are taught to say that God subjected it and that they could not have controlled it (“سبحان الذي سخر لنا هذا”); the words identify the giver of a received benefit.
luna: This neighbor completes the spoken acknowledgment begun in 43:13: “وإنا إلى ربنا لمنقلبون.” The speaker names return to the Lord after acknowledging the transport as God's gift.
terra: Pharaoh asks whether he is خَيْر than Moses, showing the same comparative-question form used as arrogant self-promotion.
terra: If asked who created them, the deniers answer “God,” so their spoken acknowledgment becomes evidence against their turning away.
terra: The question asks whether the present deniers are خَيْر or the people of Tubbaʿ, using comparison to challenge presumed security.

luna: The section gives Moses' words about the favor bestowed on him and examples of remembering divine gifts. Here a person asks God to enable gratitude for the favor given to him and his parents (“أن أشكر نعمتك”), turning recognition of favor into spoken prayer. | terra: The mature believer prays for power to thank God for blessings given to him and his parents, repeating spoken acknowledgment across generations.
terra: The question “Is this not the truth?” is answered بَلَىٰ, another explicit affirmative confirmation in response to an interrogative.
terra: God promises reward without asking believers for their wealth; 47:37 then explains the human response if such asking were pressed.
terra: If God were to ask people for wealth and press them, they would become stingy and their resentments would emerge, exposing the social tension around importunate request.

luna: The section leaves “السائل” open to a person asking for material help. 51:19 names “السائل والمحروم” among those with a due share in the believers' wealth, showing why a petitioner at the door is owed consideration. | terra: The righteous recognize in their wealth a due for لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ, treating the petitioner as a rights-bearing recipient rather than an annoyance.

luna: The verse opens Abraham's encounter with the honored guests using “هل أتاك حديث ضيف إبراهيم.” This repeats the Quranic address-form of “حديث” that the section connects with narration. | terra: The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ opens an account, again making inquiry the doorway to sequential telling.

luna: The section's dictionary note says people may ask one another. 52:25 shows the people of Paradise turning to each other to ask, making mutual conversation a peaceful scene rather than the need or rebuke of 93:10. | terra: The people of Paradise turn to one another يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, the exact reciprocal form of asking developed in the section.
terra: The reciprocal asking of 52:25 produces a personal account of how they formerly feared while among their families, beginning the promised unfolding speech.
terra: The speakers then say God favored them and protected them from the Fire, turning mutual conversation into an explicit narration of divine favor.
terra: Their account ends by recalling that they used to call upon God and by naming His goodness and mercy, completing the favor-story begun after 52:25.
terra: Immediately after the people of Paradise narrate favor in 52:25–28, the Prophet is commanded to remind, and his freedom from soothsaying or madness is attributed to بِنِعْمَتِ رَبِّكَ.
terra: The rescue of Lot’s household is called a favor from God and a recompense for gratitude, linking delivered grace to thankful response.
terra: The question asks whether the audience’s disbelievers are خَيْر than earlier peoples, a binary comparison that denies inherited exemption.
terra: Everyone in the heavens and earth asks God while He is each day bringing about a matter, joining universal petition with continuing divine response.
terra: A question, “Were we not with you?”, receives بَلَىٰ; the affirmative is genuine even though the reply then explains the fatal difference.

luna: The section allows “السائل” to be a person who comes with a question. 58:1 recounts a woman pleading and disputing her case with the Prophet, and says God hears their exchange; this is a petitioner whose speech receives attention. | terra: God hears the woman who pleads with the Prophet and her dialogue with him, making a socially vulnerable questioner’s voice heard and answered from above.
terra: After denial of resurrection, the Prophet is commanded to say بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّى and affirm both resurrection and disclosure of deeds.
terra: The possibility that God may يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ أَمْرًا closely matches the dictionary image of one thing arising after another, here as a new circumstance after waiting.
terra: A confidential حَدِيث is passed on, partly disclosed, followed by the question “Who informed you?” and its answer; one speech generates another in a complete chain.
terra: The keepers ask each arriving group whether no warner came, supplying the question answered affirmatively and then narrated in 67:9.
terra: The condemned answer بَلَىٰ and proceed to recount the warner’s coming and their denial, so an affirmative answer generates a sequential report.
terra: Their account concludes that listening or reasoning would have averted their fate, stating the consequence of refusing the warning described in 67:9.
terra: Without using خَيْر, the ayah asks which of two walkers is better guided, a concrete nonlexical parallel to asking for the preferable of two ways.
terra: The divine voice says the Prophet is not mad بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ, repeating the section’s exact attribution of blessing to his Lord.
terra: Jonah’s escape from being cast blameworthy is attributed to a blessing from his Lord, another narrated rescue with its giver named.

luna: The section's “السائل” can be someone requesting something; 70:1 describes a “سأل سائل” asking for a punishment to befall. This is a stark reversal of the vulnerable petitioner seeking help, showing that the same asking word can carry a hostile demand. | terra: A petitioner asks for the punishment bound to occur, showing that the nominal “asker” can request his own ruin and that protecting a person does not validate the requested object.

luna: The section's material reading of “السائل” is made concrete by 70:24: believers keep a known share in their wealth. Its neighbor 70:25 identifies the recipients as the petitioner and deprived person, completing the connection. | terra: A known right is established in the worshippers’ wealth; 70:25 then identifies the petitioner and deprived person as its recipients.

luna: This ayah names “السائل” and the deprived person as recipients of a known share in wealth; its neighbor 70:24 establishes that share. It directly supports the section's reading of the asker as someone seeking material help. | terra: The known right in believers’ wealth is specified as belonging to لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ, a direct counterpart to the person asking at the door.
terra: The Prophet must bear what opponents say and part from them graciously, modeling restraint under verbal injury.

luna: The section says the material “السائل” at the door is protected from rebuke. 76:8 depicts believers feeding a needy person, an orphan, and a captive, putting vulnerable recipients in the scene of giving.

luna: After 76:8 names those being fed, this ayah gives the feeders' words: “إنما نطعمكم لوجه الله” and says they seek neither repayment nor thanks. Their speech shows care for recipients without pressure or injury.

luna: The section notes the reciprocal form of asking (“تساءلوا”). 78:1 uses it of people asking one another about the great news, showing the questioner's voice can circulate among a group. | terra: The question عَمَّ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ names people asking one another, a direct occurrence of the reciprocal form developed in the prose.
terra: “The tremendous news” identifies the subject of the reciprocal questioning in 78:1, showing mutual questions organized around a report.

luna: This uses the same address as 20:9, “هل أتاك حديث موسى,” which the section cites as an example of Quranic telling. Its repetition shows that the story of Moses is introduced through direct address. | terra: The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ introduces Moses’s story and repeats the section’s meeting of question and narration.

luna: The question “متى مرساها” asks when the Hour will arrive; the answer says its timing belongs to the Lord and the Prophet is only a warner. It gives another specific boundary in response to an asker. | terra: People ask the Prophet when the Hour will be anchored; the following ayat delimit his answer while preserving his role as warner.
terra: The response to the Hour-question in 79:42 challenges any assumption that the Prophet controls its final disclosure.
terra: The endpoint of knowledge about the Hour is assigned to the Prophet’s Lord, defining the truthful limit of his answer.
terra: The Prophet’s own role is restricted to warning the one who fears it, clarifying the stance from which he answers 79:42.
terra: The frown and turning away name the adverse facial and bodily response whose correction culminates in 80:10 and parallels verbal rebuke.
terra: The blind man’s arrival identifies the vulnerable visitor whose approach occasioned the warning continued through 80:10.
terra: The possibility that the visitor might purify himself explains why a questioner seeking instruction cannot be dismissed by appearances.
terra: The possibility that a reminder might benefit him states what the seeker could receive from attentive speech.
terra: The self-sufficient person forms the social contrast to the striving seeker, exposing the status preference behind the failed reception.
terra: The Prophet’s attention to the self-sufficient person sharpens the reversal corrected by the command concerning the asker.
terra: The Prophet is told he is not responsible if that self-sufficient hearer does not purify himself, removing the rationale for neglecting the seeker.

luna: Section's “وأما السائل” protects the one who comes to ask; 80:8 itself stages the visitor “من جاءك يسعى.” Its neighbors 80:9–10 complete the scene: he fears God, while the Prophet is distracted from him. | terra: The matching وَأَمَّا construction introduces the person who comes to the Prophet striving; it is the closest parallel scene to the knowledge-seeker protected in 93:10.

luna: This neighbor to 80:8 identifies the visitor as one who “يخشى,” completing the portrait of the person who comes seeking. That detail makes the rebuke in 80:10 especially pointed beside the section's protection of the asker. | terra: The approaching person of 80:8 also fears God, identifying the seriousness of the seeker whom the Prophet must receive.

luna: The section commands that the asker not be rebuked (“فلا تنهر”). 80:10 itself reproaches the Prophet for turning away from the visitor; neighboring 80:8–9 show that he came striving and fearing God, completing the contrast with the commanded welcome. | terra: The Prophet is reproved for becoming distracted from that seeker, the narrative counterpart to the command not to rebuke the asker.

luna: The question “هل أتاك حديث الجنود” introduces the armies' story. It repeats the section's Quranic address-form in which a “حديث” is brought to the listener. | terra: The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ٱلْجُنُودِ introduces two exemplary hosts, using a question to initiate a report.
terra: People prefer the nearer worldly life, stating the mistaken choice that 87:17 corrects with the same better/later comparison as 93:4.
terra: وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ directly repeats that the Hereafter is better and adds that it is more lasting.

luna: The verse asks “هل أتاك حديث الغاشية,” introducing the account of the Overwhelming Event. It is another direct instance of the “حديث” address-form named in the section. | terra: The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ٱلْغَـٰشِيَةِ opens the coming scene through the very noun whose unfolding sense the section develops.
terra: A person interprets expanded provision by saying “My Lord has honored me,” showing that even naming the Lord can misread what a favor means.
terra: When provision is restricted, the same person says “My Lord has humiliated me,” and the next ayah’s rejection marks this speech as a false measure of divine regard.
terra: The question “Have We not expanded your breast?” addresses the Prophet with the first item in another ordered divine recounting of favors.
terra: God names removal of the Prophet’s burden as the second favor in the sequence begun at 94:1.
terra: The burden is identified by what weighed on his back, giving concrete force to the relief narrated in 94:2.
terra: God adds the raising of the Prophet’s remembrance, completing a compact succession of favors comparable to 93:6–8.
terra: The earth will تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, an explicit act of telling what happened and thus a vivid instance of the section’s command-root.

luna: The section's root note connects “نعمة” with blessing, and 102:8 says people will be questioned about “النعيم.” This places telling of favor beside accountability for what was received, a boundary to the section's command.
terra: The recipients of the surah’s favors are commanded to worship the Lord of the House, directing their response to the giver named in 106:4.
terra: The Lord is identified as the one who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear, a paired recounting of provision and shelter.

luna: The section says not to rebuke the asker, and the surrounding surah 93:9 also protects the orphan. 107:2 describes the one who repulses an orphan (“يدع اليتيم”), the opposite treatment of a vulnerable person and a sharp boundary for the section's commands.

luna: Where the section forbids harshness toward the asker and its surah context protects the orphan, 107:3 condemns failing to urge the feeding of the poor (“ولا يحض على طعام المسكين”). It supplies the material neglect that accompanies the opposite posture.
terra: God directly tells the Prophet that He has given him abundance, a concise divine narration of favor.
terra: Prayer and sacrifice are commanded as the response to the gift stated in 108:1, showing favor generating a new act and voice.
